Shaykh Ibn 'Uthaymin considers it weak, arguing that there is a single reckoning and that years are measured by the crescent moons.

Qatada and Mutarrif al-Warraq, by contrast, hold that the verse reports the words of the People of the Book, and that God refuted them when He said: God knows best how long they stayed. They rely on Ibn Mas'ud's reading, «and they said: they stayed». Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi reject this view, and Ibn 'Atiyya notes that scholars of verification regard the verse as God's own statement. Ibn 'Abbas is also reported to have seen in the difference between the two calendars the key to the passage.

On recitation, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read «three hundred years» with the noun in the genitive and no tanwin, while the majority read it with tanwin and in the accusative. Al-Tabari prefers the tanwin reading, while Abu Hayyan and others consider the construct form acceptable.

This verse says that God alone knows how long the People of the Cave stayed, that He knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth, that He sees and hears in a way beyond all creaturely perception, that no one beyond Him is a protector for the people of the heavens and the earth, and that He has no partner in His judgment. The commentators agree that the words «God knows best» refer the matter back to divine knowledge. They differ on who is speaking in «they remained». Qatada and Mutarrif al-Warraq hold that the preceding words report the claims of the People of the Book, which this verse refutes, citing Ibn Mas'ud's reading «and they said». Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-Tabari hold that it is God's own statement, with «years» explaining the three hundred. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi follow this reading and see «God knows best» as confirming the report. Ibn Abbas, in some transmissions, took the three hundred and nine years to be the claim of the people, a view Ibn Kathir finds weak. For the extra nine years, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that they are the gap between solar and lunar years. Transmissions from Ibn Abbas say the sleepers were seven, with their dog as the eighth. Readers also differ on whether «three hundred» is read with tanwin or as an construct. The central message stays the same: knowledge belongs to God alone, and He alone is the protector and the judge.

God commands His Prophet Muhammad to recite the Book revealed to him and to follow its commands, prohibitions and rulings, never abandoning it, for whoever opposes it will end in Hell. The commentators affirm that no one can alter or change the words of God, and that only He has that power; if the Prophet were to deviate, he would find no refuge apart from God. Mujahid and Qatada explain the word multahad as refuge or shelter, Ibn Abbas as a safe place, al-Hasan as an entrance, and others as a place of escape or turning away. Al-Mawardi notes that these meanings are close, and that the root conveys the idea of leaning towards something. The scholars differ on what the words denote: al-Tabari takes them as God's threats against those who disobey, while others take them as the Quran itself, or as both its reports and its rulings. Al-Razi argues that abrogation is not truly a substitution, since the abrogated ruling remains in force until the abrogating one arrives. On the occasion of the following verse, most commentators report that it was revealed when leading men of Quraysh asked the Prophet to send away poor believers such as Salman, Bilal and Khabbab. God then commanded him to keep himself with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face, and not to obey the one whose heart God has made heedless of His remembrance. Opinions differ on the calling meant: for some it is the obligatory prayer, for others the congregational prayer, and for others remembrance and supplication in general.

In this verse God commands His Prophet ﷺ to restrain himself and remain with the poor believers who call on their Lord morning and evening, seeking only His face, and not to let his eyes turn from them toward the wealthy in pursuit of the adornment of worldly life. He also forbids him to obey the one whose heart God has made heedless of His remembrance, who follows his desire and whose affair is ruined. The commentators agree that these believers are the poor Companions such as Bilal, Ammar, Suhayb and Ibn Mas'ud, and that calling upon the Lord morning and evening refers either to the prayers or to constant remembrance. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn 'Umar take it to mean the five daily prayers, Qatada the dawn and afternoon prayers, while al-Tabari and others understand it as continual invocation. Regarding the occasion of revelation, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that leading Meccans asked the Prophet to send these believers away, while other reports name 'Uyayna ibn Hisn and al-Aqra' or Umayya ibn Khalaf. Scholars differ on the meaning of furutan: loss according to Mujahid and al-Tabari, regret according to Dawud, excess according to Muqatil, neglected according to al-Farra'. On whether God is the one who makes the heart heedless, the Mu'tazilites such as al-Zamakhshari read it as a finding or a naming, whereas the Sunni commentators, including al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim, take it as a divine action, a point belonging to the theological debate.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ to say to the people that the truth comes from their Lord, so whoever wills may believe and whoever wills may disbelieve. The commentators agree that this is a warning and a threat rather than a genuine choice, as the verses that follow describe the punishment of the wrongdoers. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd read it as a threat, al-Zajjaj as a warning rather than a command, and al-Mawardi explains that God gains nothing from people's faith and is not harmed by their disbelief. Al-Tabari reports Ibn 'Abbas as saying that whoever God wills to have faith believes, and whoever He wills to disbelieve disbelieves. Al-Razi and the Mu'tazila debated from this verse the question of human freedom: the Mu'tazila saw in it the independence of the servant in his choice, while Sunni theologians replied that the human will itself depends on God's will.

The wrongdoers are, for most commentators, the disbelievers. Ibn 'Abbas says the enclosure of the fire (suradiq) is a wall of fire surrounding them, while Qatada and Ibn Qutayba describe it as smoke or a tent-like enclosure, and Ibn Kathir cites a hadith about its four thick walls, which some scholars consider weak in its chain. The meaning of al-Muhl varies: Ibn 'Abbas says it is thick water like the dregs of olive oil, Mujahid says pus and blood, Ibn Mas'ud and Abu 'Ubayda say any molten metal, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr says water whose heat has reached its limit. Al-Tabari notes that these views are close in meaning. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi see irony in the fact that such people are given water to drink in answer to their plea. As for murtafaq, Ibn 'Abbas explains it as a dwelling, Mujahid as a gathering, and Abu 'Ubayda as a reclining place. Several scholars note that the word is used here in contrast with the description of the garden, since the people of the fire have no real rest.

This verse states that God will not waste the reward of those who believe and do righteous deeds, and that they will have the Gardens of Eden, with rivers flowing beneath them. They will be adorned with gold bracelets, wear green garments of fine silk (sundus) and thick brocade (istabraq), and recline on couches. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the answer to 'those who believe' to be 'for them are the Gardens of Eden', and see the clause 'We do not waste the reward' as a parenthetical emphasis; Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi agree. Al-Zajjaj suggests the clause itself may be the predicate, meaning 'we do not waste their reward', while the Akhfash treats 'the one who did good deeds' as the linking element, since it refers in meaning to the believers. Al-Tabari notes that the repetition of 'inna' is for emphasis and cites a well-known line of verse. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi point out that 'the one who does good' in effect means the believers who act righteously. On the ornaments, Sa'id ibn Jubayr mentions three bracelets of gold, silver and pearls, while others keep to gold as the text states. Lexicographers distinguish sundus, a fine silk, from istabraq, a thicker silk. A hadith cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, whose chain is debated, links the verse to the four early caliphs; al-Qurtubi reports it without judgement. The commentators agree that this promise follows the warning to the disbelievers and is read as a counterpart to it.

This verse describes the reward of those who believe and do righteous deeds: gardens of Eden, meaning lasting dwelling, with rivers flowing beneath them. They will be adorned with gold bracelets, clothed in green garments of fine silk (sundus) and thick silk (istabraq), and will recline on couches in canopied chambers. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Razi and al-Baydawi, explain that 'adn' means a settled abode, and that the plural 'gardens' reflects the vastness of Paradise. The phrase 'We do not waste the reward of one who does good' is a parenthetical statement that reinforces the meaning. On the bracelets, most keep to gold, but Sa'id ibn Jubayr says each person receives three, of gold, silver and pearls, a view Ibn al-Jawzi also reports. Most understand sundus as thin brocade and istabraq as the thicker kind, though some, such as Abu Imran al-Jawni, take istabraq to be silk woven with gold. The arā'ik are couches within canopies, according to Qatada and Ibn Abbas. Some exegetes, including al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi, link the verse to the Companions of the Prophet, but this is not held by all. All agree that the reward is excellent and the dwelling a fine place of rest, set against the fire described just before.

In this verse God sets out a parable for the proud notables who asked the Prophet ﷺ to send away the poor believers. He describes two men: to one, the arrogant disbeliever, He gave two gardens of grapevines surrounded by palm trees, with crops between them, so that both gardens yielded their produce in full without any loss, and a river flowed through them. The commentators explain that the word thamar in the plural reading means abundant wealth, according to Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, who specify gold, silver and all kinds of property, whereas Ibn Zayd took it to mean the root that bears the fruit. Al-Tabari adopts the reading of the majority, which means fruits. All agree that the rich man boasted over his believing companion of his wealth and his strength in numbers, his nafar, which some understand as servants and kin and others as male children. Entering his garden while wronging himself through disbelief, he thought it would never perish, denied the Hour, and claimed that if he were returned to his Lord he would find something better. As to the identity of the two men, al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and others report that they were two Israelite brothers who inherited eight thousand dinars, while al-Kalbi and Ibn Atiyya identify them as two brothers from the Banu Makhzum in Mecca. Al-Mawardi also suggests the parable may be a general one with no historical event behind it, which Ibn Atiyya considers less likely. Ibn Kathir holds that the parable targets the arrogant rich man, without settling the question of who the two men were.

This verse describes two gardens that both yielded their fruit in full, without any shortfall, with a river flowing between them. The commentators explain that these were vineyards surrounded by palm trees, with crops growing in between, making them among the finest and most productive estates. Most of them, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari, agree that "kilta" means each of the two gardens, that the verb "atat" is in the singular because the word itself is singular, and that "lam tazlim minhu shay'an" means they lost none of their produce, unlike ordinary orchards whose yield varies from year to year. On the water, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi note that the river ran inside the gardens, and that the intensive form "fajjarna" expresses the abundance of the flow.

The meaning of "thamar" is disputed. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean wealth, gold and silver or goods of every kind, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as the fruit of the trees, and Ibn Zayd as the roots of the plantations. Al-Baydawi takes it as various kinds of property beyond the two gardens. Grammatical debates also concern "kilta": al-Farra' considers it a dual, while the Basran grammarians treat it as a singular word with a dual sense, a point Ibn al-Qayyim sets out at length.

The commentators report that the owner of the gardens spoke to his companion with pride, boasting of his wealth and his kin. They see in these words a sign of arrogance, without settling the identity of the two men or whether the account is a real event or an example given for instruction.

In this verse God describes the owner of the two gardens, an unbelieving man who boasts to his believing companion that he has more wealth and a mightier following, meaning more relatives, servants and supporters. The commentators read the word thamar in two main ways. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean wealth in general, gold, silver and other property, while others, including al-Farra' and Ibn Kathir, take it to mean fruit and produce, Ibn Kathir finding this more apparent here. The readings differ in their vowels, and the readers' usage explains both senses. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the damma reading is the best known, and that the two meanings lie close together. On the dialogue, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi see an opposition between faith and disbelief, and between desire for this world and desire for the next, while others understand it as the believer's admonition met by the unbeliever's arrogance. Most exegetes treat the account as an old story, reported either about Israelite brothers or about Meccans. Al-Mawardi presents it as a parable for this community, meant to encourage renunciation of the world. What the commentators share is the lesson that pride in wealth and kin turns a person from God, and that riches do not show a person's worth before Him.

This verse describes the owner of two gardens entering his orchard while wronging himself through his disbelief. He says he does not think this garden will ever perish, does not think the Hour will come, and claims that if he is returned to his Lord he will find something better than it. The commentators agree that his wronging of himself is his unbelief and denial of resurrection, and that his words "never" mean a long duration rather than literal eternity. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi connect his confidence to the beauty of the trees, fruits, fields and flowing rivers he sees. The verse speaks of one garden although he owns two, because he enters only one at a time. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the words were spoken in the presence of a believing companion, and they treat them as doubt about the return and a wish placed upon God. Al-Zamakhshari reads them as an oath resting on the idea that he deserved his wealth, while Ibn Ashur reads them as mockery of his companion. Readers differ on whether the pronoun should be "minhuma" referring to both gardens or "minha" referring to the one he entered. Several commentators, including al-Razi, note that he failed to understand that worldly wealth is no sign of honour in the hereafter. The differences concern the identity of the persons and the readings of the text rather than the general meaning of the verse.

This verse of Surat al-Kahf reports the words of the owner of the two gardens, the disbelieving man of the parable, who entered his garden and was impressed by its fruits, trees and rivers. He says he does not think this garden will ever perish, nor that the Hour will come; and if he is returned to his Lord, as his believing companion says, he expects to find something better than his garden in this world. The commentators agree that he wronged himself through his disbelief, his doubt about resurrection and his pride, and that his words amount to presumption toward God. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that this is doubt about resurrection, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi consider that the word 'this' may refer to the garden or to all of creation. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the garden is mentioned in the singular because he entered only one of the two, and that he has no share in the garden promised to the righteous. They also record the readings 'minhuma' and 'minha', both accepted in different regions. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi report that the man had grown rich and boasted over his poor believing brother, and they mention various traditions about his wealth and the origin of the parable. Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress that wealth and kin are no proof of worth, and that assuming the favour of this world will repeat in the next is faulty reasoning. Overall, the commentators read the verse as a warning against the pride that prosperity can breed, while differing on the precise sense of the wording and on the identity of those involved.

This passage records the words of the believing man to his unbelieving companion as they argued. He rebukes him for denying the One who created him first from dust, then from a drop of semen, and then shaped him into a complete, upright man. Most commentators understand the dust to refer to Adam, the origin of all mankind. The rebuke also carries an argument for resurrection: the One who could create at the beginning can recreate. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain that the man became an unbeliever through his doubt about the resurrection and about God's full power. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy link it to the same denial of resurrection. Others, such as al-Alusi, consider that he may have been a polytheist, relying on the believer's statement that he associates no one with his Lord. The readings differ on the word "lakinna": Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read it with an alif in connected speech, while most readers omit it there, and all agree on the alif when pausing. Al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas explain that it derives from "lakin ana", with the hamza dropped and the two nuns assimilated. Ibn Kathir and others cite hadiths on the merit of saying "there is no power except in God" when a blessing is seen, a formula the believer had urged on his companion. The details of the garden's fate and the outcome for the unbeliever are described in various ways by the commentators, and no single reading is decisively preferred.

This verse records the believing man's reply to his companion, who denied the Resurrection and trusted in his garden. The believer rebukes him by reminding him that God created his origin from dust, then from a drop of semen, then shaped him into a complete man, and then declares: 'But as for me, He is God, my Lord, and I associate no one with my Lord.' The commentators agree on the general meaning: the believer corrects his companion's denial and affirms the oneness and lordship of God alone. They also agree on the argument behind the reply: the One who created man at first can bring him back again. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir develop this reasoning, Ibn Kathir noting that every creature knows it was once nonexistent and so must acknowledge its Creator. The main disagreements concern the reading and grammar of the word 'lakinna'. Al-Tabari judges the reading that keeps the alif only in pause to be the correct one, and considers the alif in connection to be poor Arabic. Ibn Amir reads it with the alif in both cases, which al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy explain as compensation for the dropped hamza. Al-Kisai, reported by al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, proposes a reversal of word order, meaning 'but God is my Lord'. Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi detail further variants in pronouns and forms. As for the closing words, al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy read them as an indirect rebuke of the companion's association of others with God, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi understand them as a refusal to measure wealth and poverty by anything other than God's will.

The poor believer tells his wealthy companion that when he enters his garden and is impressed by it, he should say: 'What God wills; there is no power except through God.' Commentators treat this as both a rebuke and a piece of advice. They differ on the grammar of 'ma': al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baydawi read it as a relative pronoun meaning 'the matter is what God wills', while others take it as a conditional whose answer is implied. Al-Qurtubi reports that Malik advised saying this on entering one's home. The believer then hopes that God will give him something better than that garden, in this world or the next, and will send down on his companion's garden a punishment from the sky, leaving it a bare, slippery ground, or will sink its water so deep that it cannot be reached. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take 'husban' as a punishment, Ibn Kathir specifically as a violent rain; Ibn Qutayba and Abu 'Ubayda take it as projectiles or thunderbolts, while al-Zajjaj reads it as the reckoning of what your hands have earned. The rich man then regrets and wrings his hands, wishing he had not associated anyone with God. The commentators do not agree on the sincerity of this repentance: al-Razi says his regret was over losing his wealth, and that his belief in God was not disinterested.

The verse records the words of the steadfast believer to his disbelieving companion, who was proud of his garden. He tells him that if he sees him as having less wealth and fewer children, he hopes his Lord will give him something better than that garden, either in this world or in the hereafter, and will send upon the garden a punishment from heaven that turns it into a bare, slippery ground where no foot can stand, or will let its water sink so deep that it cannot be reached. The commentators agree that husban here means a punishment, as Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak report, while Ibn Zayd understands it as a divine decree. Al-Zajjaj, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir note that it can also mean reckoning, that is, the punishment matching what your hands have earned. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi report that it refers to projectiles, which some take to be thunderbolts, others hail or stones, and Abu Zayd al-Kilabi says it means locusts. All agree that sa'id means the surface of the earth and zalaq means ground where feet slip, expressing the complete loss of plants and buildings. Following at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, ghawran is a verbal noun used as an adjective meaning sunk into the earth. Ibn Ashur holds that the prayer targets the complete destruction of the garden. The scholars differ on which good is hoped for: al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir place it in the hereafter, while others take it to refer to this world or to both, and God knows best.

This passage of Surah al-Kahf describes the poor believer who warns his arrogant, wealthy companion, the owner of two gardens. The believer says that God may send upon that garden a punishment from the sky, turning it into bare, slippery ground where no foot can stand, or may cause its water to sink deep into the earth so that no one can reach it. The commentators broadly agree that husban means a punishment or calamity: Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn 'Abbas take it to mean a chastisement, Ibn Zayd a divine decree, while al-Akhfash and Abu 'Ubayda explain it as a volley of projectiles or thunderbolts. Al-Zajjaj connects it with reckoning, meaning the requital of what your hands have earned. The word ghawr, meaning water that has sunk away, is for most of them a verbal noun used as an adjective, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note the emphasis this form carries. Ibn Kathir and others see in this passage the believer's prayer against his companion's garden and his hope placed in God. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi recall that one should say, when something pleases you, 'As God wills; there is no power except through God', and al-Qurtubi cites several hadiths on the merit of this formula. The variant readings do not change the general meaning, which all the commentators place within the same frame of requital and the reminder of God's power.

This verse describes the fate of the owner of the two gardens after his believing companion's warning comes true: his fruit is destroyed, and he begins to wring his hands in regret over what he had spent on the gardens, whose trellises have collapsed and whose land lies in ruin. He then cries out that he wished he had never associated anyone with his Lord. Commentators agree that wringing the hands is a figure of speech for deep regret and anguish. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the cry as regret for having disbelieved, while al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi understand it as grief over the loss of his wealth, since he had been sure the gardens would never perish. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur allow both readings, and suggest it may be a late repentance. All agree that the destruction of the fruit means total ruin. The reciters differ on the word for fruit and on whether the verb is read with ta or ya, without changing the meaning. Al-Qurtubi notes that the disaster seems to have struck at night, while others take the verb to mean simply 'became'. Ibn Sa'di and al-Jaza'iri stress that this remorse comes too late to save anything.

This part of the verse says that the owner of the two gardens, who had been proud of his wealth and his followers, had no group to help him against God's punishment, and could not defend himself by his own strength. The commentators agree that "fi'a" means a group, a clan or a troop: Mujahid says it refers to his clan, while al-Kalbi and al-Baghawi understand it as soldiers or a band, and Qatada explains "muntasir" as one who protects himself. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di draw the lesson that those who boast of their wealth and supporters are left alone when punishment comes. On grammar, Sibawayh takes "yansurunahu" as a description of "fi'a", whereas al-Mubarrad takes it as the predicate; al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan report this disagreement. On recitation, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur note that both the feminine and masculine readings of the verb are permitted. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a warning against those who take pride in worldly goods and look down on poor believers, and he stresses that the punishment fell because of arrogance and not disbelief alone. Al-Tabari discusses the readings only in connection with the following verse.

The commentators connect this verse to the story of the two men with the two gardens. When the disbeliever's garden is destroyed and he regrets his association of others with God, no group helps him apart from God, and he cannot defend himself. Most read 'there' as referring to that moment and state, while Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi also take it to mean the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari explain that guardianship belongs to God alone at that time, that He alone holds victory and sovereignty, and that He is best in rewarding and in the final outcome. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari take the fatha reading of wilaya as aid and allegiance, and the kasra reading as power and rule; al-Tabari prefers the kasra, while Ibn Kathir reads the fatha as everyone turning back to God when punishment comes. On 'al-haqq', the genitive reading makes it a description of God, the nominative a description of the guardianship, and the accusative an emphatic complement. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that Abu 'Amr and al-Asma'i considered the kasra an error, but Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari answer that the reading is transmitted. For 'uqban', the readings with a damma or a sukun share the meaning of final outcome. Ibn Sa'di draws the lesson not to be intoxicated by wealth and to say 'what God wills', while Ibn 'Ashur sees in the verse a general conclusion that any protection other than God's is vain.

God tells His Prophet to set before the arrogant a likeness of worldly life: it is like water sent down from the sky, through which the plants of the earth grow thick and flourish, until they dry up, crumble, and are scattered by the winds. God is capable of all things, both bringing into being and bringing to an end. The commentators agree that the image shows how quickly the life of this world passes after its splendour, and warns against being deceived by it. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the verse was addressed to those who wanted the poor believers driven away. Views differ on the preposition in 'bihi': al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi take it to mean that the water mingled with the plants until they were saturated, while others take it to mean that the plants intermingled because of the water. On the sense of 'asbaha', Abu Hayyan, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi read it as 'became' without restricting it to morning. The variant readings of 'tadhruhu' do not change the meaning, according to Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi. The verse then turns to wealth and children, which are the adornment of worldly life, while the enduring good deeds are better with God in reward and in hope. The commentators differ on what these good deeds are: Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say the five prayers, the majority say the formulas of remembrance, and in another report Ibn 'Abbas says any good deed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di prefer the broadest reading.

The commentators explain that this verse likens the life of this world to water sent down from the sky, which makes plants grow until they dry into stubble that the winds scatter. Wealth and children are described as a passing adornment of worldly life, not provision for the Hereafter. Most agree that the 'enduring good deeds' are acts of goodness whose reward remains, but they differ on what exactly they are. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Amr ibn Shurahbil, Masruq and Ibrahim, as well as Abu Maysara, identify them with the five daily prayers. Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Mujahid and al-Dahhak, and the majority of exegetes according to Abu Hayyan, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, identify them with the formulas of glorifying God, praising Him, affirming His oneness and His greatness, some adding 'there is no power nor strength except in God', a view also attributed to Uthman, Ibn Umar and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. Al-Tabari holds that they include all good deeds, a view Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud also favour. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi define them as good deeds whose fruit endures, al-Hasan as sincere intentions, and Qatada as any deed done for God's sake. As for 'better hope', most explain that the one who does these deeds hopes for God's reward in this life and finds it in the next, while al-Mawardi sees it as the truest hope because it never deceives. Al-Shinqiti concludes that all these views come back to one thing: the deeds that please God.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when the mountains are set in motion and the earth is seen laid bare, with no mountain, tree or building covering it, and when all creatures are gathered so that not one of them is left behind. The commentators agree on the core meaning: the end of the order of this world and the open, levelled surface of the earth. They differ on how the mountains are moved. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi say they are removed from their places and pass like clouds, while al-Mawardi offers three readings: their displacement, their reduction until little remains, or their turning into scattered dust. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi hold that they are ultimately annihilated, and al-Alusi reports that some see a sequence of stages. On the baring of the earth, al-Tabari and Ata take it to mean that what lies within it, the dead, come forth, a view Ibn Kathir regards as possible, whereas most exegetes, including Mujahid, Qatada and al-Razi, understand simply that the earth is exposed. On the phrase 'We left none of them behind', Ibn Qutayba and al-Tabari explain it as not leaving anyone behind, and al-Baydawi as not abandoning anyone. Regarding the presentation in rows, some take it as a single line, others as successive ranks, and al-Razi as a gathering in which no one hides another. The commentators read 'You have come to Us' as a rebuke addressed to those who denied the resurrection, not to the believers.

This verse describes the scene of the Day of Resurrection, when all creatures are presented before their Lord in ranks, with no one hidden from another. They are then rebuked: they have come as He created them the first time, naked and alone, without wealth or children, and they once claimed that God would never set an appointment for their resurrection. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the gathering as the summoning of all beings for judgment. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir note that the word saff may mean successive rows, like those of prayer, or a single line, and Ibn Kathir supports his view with hadiths. The commentators generally agree on the sense of “as the first time”, but differ on its meaning: al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi take it to mean barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi see mainly a rebuke for their pride in wealth and allies. For al-Tabari, the words “bal za'amtum” are addressed to the unbelievers, though the wording is general. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Shinqiti read “bal” as a shift from one statement to another rather than a cancellation. Thus the verse remains a rebuke for denying the resurrection, which the commentators connect with the warning of a certain judgment.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when the Book of deeds is set down and the guilty, terrified by what it contains, cry out in dismay and marvel at a record that leaves no small or great act uncounted. The commentators agree that the Book refers to the record of deeds handed to each person, at the right hand or the left, and that it contains everything done in this world, so that each finds his deeds present before him and cannot deny them. They also agree that God does none wrong: He does not record what was not done and does not add to a deserved punishment.

Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the "small" and "great" sins are the sins in general, while Ibn 'Abbas explains the small as a smile and the great as loud laughter, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr explains the small as touching and kissing and the great as fornication. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi present these as examples rather than a closed list. Al-Qurtubi and al-Razi stress caution against minor sins, since they lead to major ones, and Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi cite the hadith comparing small faults to gathered firewood that eventually kindles a fire.

Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud note that the Book may mean several records or one comprehensive register, and that the past tense conveys the certainty of the event. On these points the commentators leave the choice open rather than deciding between the readings.

This verse recalls that God commanded the angels to prostrate before Adam in honour, and all of them did except Iblis, who was of the jinn and thereby departed from his Lord's command. God then asks the people how they can take Iblis and his offspring as allies, when they are enemies to them, calling this an evil exchange for wrongdoers. The commentators agree that the verse warns against obeying Satan and reminds believers of his long-standing enmity towards Adam and his children. They differ over Iblis's origin. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi hold that he was of the jinn and not of the angels, relying on the literal wording, and Ibn Kathir cites al-Hasan saying he was never an angel even for a moment. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi discuss several positions, including that Iblis was an angel or that the jinn were a kind of angel to which he belonged. Ibn Atiyya and al-Nasafi take a middle view. On the meaning of fisq, al-Farra and Ibn Qutayba explain it as going out of obedience, while al-Zajjaj reports that God's command was the cause of his disobedience. On Iblis's offspring, Qatada and Ibn Zayd say they multiply as humans do, whereas many detailed accounts of his children and their roles are judged unreliable by Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Shinqiti. Al-Razi finally links the story to the reproach of the wealthy who looked down on poor believers, just as Iblis looked down on Adam.

This verse says that God did not have Iblis and his offspring witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of one another, and that He never took the misleaders as helpers. From this the commentators draw that it is wrong to take Satan and his descendants as allies instead of God. They agree on the core point: these beings have no share in creation or in governing, and only the Creator deserves worship. Qatada, as cited by al-Tabari, explains that the devils lead the children of Adam astray and do not guide them to rectitude, and al-Tabari adds that the term may also cover misled human followers. On the pronoun in 'I did not make them witness', opinions differ. Al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya refer it to Iblis and his offspring, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi refer it to the disbelievers who demanded that the poor believers be driven away from the Prophet. Al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi extend it to the polytheists or even to all people, which would target astrologers and physicians who claim knowledge of creation. Ibn 'Atiyya keeps Iblis and his offspring as the primary target and sees the other groups as included. Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir note that helpers need not be present at creation. Abu Hayyan also records a reading in the second person addressing the Prophet. The passage then describes the Day when God tells the associators to call on their supposed partners, who do not respond, and places a 'mawbiq' between them. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it as a valley in Hell, al-Hasan as enmity, Ibn Kathir as a separation, and al-Razi as a deep barrier. Finally the guilty see the Fire and think they will fall into it. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada read the verb as certainty, while others take it as expectation given the terrifying roar they hear.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when God tells the polytheists to call upon those they claimed were His partners. They call on them for help, but the partners do not answer or aid them. God then says: and We place between them a mawbiq. Most commentators understand this as a place of ruin or destruction, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak. Others take it to be a deep valley in Hell, a view attributed to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, Anas and Mujahid. Al-Hasan al-Basri reads it as enmity, and Abu 'Ubayda as an appointed meeting place. Al-Farra' explains that the ties they formed in this world become their ruin in the next. As for the criminals seeing the Fire and thinking they will fall into it, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi take the word zann to mean certain knowledge, while others hold that they see it from afar and immediately believe they will be thrown into it, citing a hadith from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri about the distance of forty years. Finally, they find no escape, for the Fire surrounds them on every side. The commentators broadly agree on the hopeless state of the polytheists, but differ on the meaning of mawbiq and of zann.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when the criminals, meaning the polytheists, see the Fire and become certain that they will be cast into it, finding no escape and no place to turn to. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, understand the word zanna here to mean certainty rather than mere suspicion. Ibn Kathir adds that this foretaste of punishment increases their distress. As for masrif, al-Tabari, Ibn Qutayba and al-Qurtubi explain it as a way out or a refuge, citing a line of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir connect the passage to the mawbiq, the barrier or abyss that separates the idolaters from their partners, presenting the whole scene as the total failure of those who turned away from God. Al-Alusi, al-Shawkani and Abu al-Su'ud note a different possibility: that the sinners, seeing the Fire from afar, only believed it would seize them at once. Ibn 'Ashur sees a note of irony in the use of zanna, since they are in fact certain of their fate. The commentators do not settle the precise nature of the vision and leave it open.

In this verse God states that He has varied in this Quran the examples, lessons and proofs given to people, so that they might remember, turn back to Him, abandon polytheism and heed admonition. Yet man, more than anything else, is prone to dispute and contention, not yielding to the truth nor restrained by warning, as al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir explain. Several commentators, including al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy, take the word "man" here to mean disbelievers or polytheists, and name al-Nadr ibn al-Harith or Ubayy ibn Khalaf as those intended. Al-Baghawi nonetheless concludes that the meaning is general, which he regards as the sounder view. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan read "jadalan" as a specifying accusative, meaning that human argumentativeness exceeds that of any other thing. Al-Razi notes that the prophets themselves debated with their peoples, which implies a two-sided exchange. Ibn 'Ashur observes that disputation is not always blameworthy, since it can be praiseworthy as with Abraham, but that the context here concerns argument in falsehood. Ibn 'Uthaymin cites Ibn Mas'ud's saying that peoples who indulged in controversy went astray, and stresses that the believer submits to the truth. Ibn Sa'di holds that such contention stems from injustice and obstinacy rather than from any lack of clarity in the message.

This verse rebukes people for refusing to believe and to seek forgiveness after the guidance has reached them. The commentators agree that the obstacle was not a lack of clarity but their stubbornness and their demand to see the punishment that struck earlier nations, or to witness it face to face. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that they demanded to see the punishment with their own eyes, as the peoples of Hud and Shu'ayb did. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi hold that a word is omitted, so that the sense is the waiting for the custom of the ancients to come upon them. Al-Zajjaj reads it as a request for that custom. On the meaning of 'qubulan', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Zayd take it as 'face to face, in plain view', Mujahid as 'suddenly', while al-Farra' and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as the plural of 'qabil', meaning various kinds of punishment. The recitations differ between the vowelled forms. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy identify the divine will as the real barrier. The scholars agree that the verse rebukes these people, that messengers are bringers of good news and warners rather than compellers, and that one who persists in wrongdoing is deprived of guidance. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi apply the verse to the Quraysh, while al-Wahidi applies it to the idolaters slain at Badr and Uhud.

This verse states that the messengers were sent only to bring good news to believers and warnings to disbelievers, yet those who disbelieve argue with falsehood in order to overturn the truth, and mock God's signs and the warnings they received. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the disputing as the polytheists' challenges to the Prophet, such as their questions about the People of the Cave, the soul, or their demands for signs. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi broaden this to include objections such as 'he is only a human' and denial of resurrection. All the commentators explain the verb 'to overturn' as meaning to remove or nullify, its root being slipping. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that 'what they were warned of' can be read as a relative clause or as a verbal noun, and gloss 'mockery' as ridicule, with a reading that uses sukun. Ibn 'Ashur sees the argument as stubbornness that does not seek guidance. Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin draw the lesson that anyone who argues to dismiss the truth shares this trait. Several commentators, including al-Mawardi and Abu Hayyan, connect the verse to the rejection of guidance and the punishments mentioned around it.

This verse states that no one is more unjust than a person who is reminded of the signs of his Lord, turns away from them, and forgets what his hands have sent forward of disbelief and sins. The commentators understand the signs to be the Quran. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi take forgetting to mean neglecting and not repenting rather than losing memory. God explains that He has placed coverings over their hearts so they cannot understand, and deafness in their ears, so that even when called to guidance they will never be guided. The commentators agree that stubborn aversion leads to being deprived of understanding. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that it refers to particular people whom God knew would not believe, while Ibn 'Atiyya reads it more generally and notes that some did later accept faith. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that the call itself will not benefit them, and that the conditional clause answers the Prophet's eagerness to guide them. On the meaning of the coverings, Ibn al-Qayyim cites Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, who compare them to a quiver or a sheath, while Ibn 'Ashur reads them as a metaphor. Al-Razi notes the apparent tension with texts on human responsibility without deciding between the positions. The following verses speak of God's forgiveness and His delay of punishment, of an appointed term for the wrongdoers, and of the cities destroyed for their injustice. Commentators differ on that term: some say Badr, others the Day of Resurrection or death.

The commentators explain that God, out of His forgiveness and mercy, does not hasten punishment upon the disbelievers for what they have earned, but sets for them an appointed time from which they will find no refuge. Most understand al-Ghafur as the one of abundant forgiveness and Dhu al-Rahma as the one possessed of mercy. The exegetes give several meanings to mercy, including pardon, reward, favour and guidance. Al-Mawardi holds that it covers believers and disbelievers in this world, while others restrict it to believers in the sense of pardon and reward.

Most agree that the mawʿid is a fixed time for the punishment, but they differ on what it is. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi identify it as the day of Badr or the Day of Reckoning, al-Razi and al-Nasafi mention Badr or the Day of Resurrection, and Ibn al-Jawzi also reports death or the punishment of the hereafter. The word mawʾil means a refuge or a place of safety, and the commentators quote Arabic verses to illustrate it, notably al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda.

The commentators also read the verse as a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ and a warning to the Meccans, before moving to the destroyed towns mentioned next. The reading of the word (li-mahlikihim) varies in its vowels, and Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nahhas and al-Zajjaj explain that its meaning shifts between a time and the act of destruction. Some modern authors present these views without choosing between them.

This verse states that the towns Allah destroyed, such as the peoples of 'Ad, Thamud, Lot and Madyan, were destroyed when their inhabitants did wrong by disbelieving, and that Allah had set an appointed time for their destruction that neither came early nor late. Al-Tabari explains that the phrase really means the people of those towns, the sentence following the sense rather than the word 'towns', and he cites some grammarians of Basra on this point. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the warning to be addressed to the disbelievers of Quraysh: just as those peoples were destroyed at their set time, these too have an appointed time from which they cannot escape. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that this appointment may refer to the day of Badr or the conquest, or to the hour of death or the punishment of the Hereafter. The commentators agree that the destruction came because of wrongdoing and that Allah was the one who decreed it. On the recitation, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi report that most readers said 'limuhlikihim' with a damma on the mim, that Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read 'limahlakihim' with fatha on both letters, and that Hafs read 'limahlikihim'. Al-Tabari prefers the majority reading, since all the readers accepted it and since the preceding verb is 'we destroyed them'. These views converge: Allah does not hasten the punishment, but when the appointed time comes it does not delay.

This verse records Moses saying to his attendant and disciple Yusha ibn Nun that he will not stop walking until he reaches the meeting place of the two seas, or spends a long time traveling in search of a righteous servant whom God told him knows more than he does. Commentators agree that the Moses meant is Moses son of Imran and that the young man is Yusha, and that the literal sense of 'la abrah' is 'I will not cease', with the predicate understood from the journey. On the location of the meeting of the two seas opinions differ: al-Tabari, Qatada and Mujahid take it to be where the sea of Persia meets the sea of Rome, Muhammad ibn Kab al-Qurazi places it near Tangier, and Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and others mention Ifriqiya or the Andalusian sea. Some, including al-Zamakhshari, read the two seas as Moses and al-Khidr, though most commentators consider this weak. The word 'huqub' is also variously explained: Ibn Abbas says a long age, Ibn Umar eighty years, Mujahid seventy, and Qatada and Ibn Zayd an indefinite period. The reports relate that Moses, asked who was the most learned man, answered 'I', and God rebuked him and announced a servant more learned than him at the meeting of the two seas, with the sign being the loss of a fish. Commentators note that the forgetting is attributed to both travelers although it was the young man who forgot. The main lessons drawn are the value of seeking knowledge, humility before the teacher, and that a prophet is not obliged to know everything.

The commentators explain that Moses, together with his servant Yusha' ibn Nun, reached the meeting place of the two seas, where he had been told he would find the righteous servant. They forgot the fish they had carried as provision, and it made its way into the sea. The exegetes note that the forgetting is attributed to both of them, though only the servant was responsible, in line with the Arabic custom of ascribing an act to a group. On how the fish made its path, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes say the water parted over the fish's track and stayed like an arch, relying on the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b; Qatada says the water froze along the route; Ibn 'Abbas in another report says the place became solid rock; Ibn Zayd holds that the path was first made on land before the fish reached the sea. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that Moses marvelled at this sign when he returned to the spot. The narrative continues with the hunger and fatigue that overtook them after passing the place; Moses asked for food, and the servant recalled what had happened to the fish, which alerted Moses that the goal was near. They retraced their steps and found al-Khadir. Scholars differ on his status: most consider him a prophet, others a righteous servant. Some hold that the forgetting was an absent-minded lapse rather than neglect, and that it carried a wisdom. The passage teaches the value of seeking knowledge, travelling to acquire it, and the humility of the learned man before one who holds knowledge he lacks.

This passage tells that after Moses and his young companion Yusha' passed the meeting point of the two seas, where Moses had been promised a meeting with a righteous servant of God, Moses felt hunger and weariness. He asked his companion to bring their morning meal. The companion then remembered that the fish they had taken as provision had slipped into the sea, and that he had forgotten to tell Moses. The commentators agree that the fish was a sign God gave Moses to recognise the place where he would meet al-Khidr, and that the forgetting is attributed to both because both had taken the provision. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that Moses only felt the fatigue after passing the place he had been told, which served as a reminder for him to turn back. On how the fish escaped, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada say the water froze along its path and formed a kind of tunnel, al-Kalbi reports that Yusha' had washed in the spring of life and the water revived the fish, and others give other meanings to the word sarab. Opinions differ on where the two seas meet: Qatada places it between the sea of Persia and the Roman sea, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi near Tangier, Ubayy ibn Ka'b in Ifriqiya, and some take the two seas to be Moses and al-Khidr. On the word huqub, Ibn 'Abbas understands it as a long age, Ibn 'Umar as eighty years, and Mujahid as seventy years. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the companion's second forgetting concerns reporting the event rather than memory itself, and that attributing it to Satan is a mark of courtesy.

In this verse, Moses' attendant Yusha' ibn Nun tells Moses about the moment they rested by the rock: he says he forgot the fish they had brought as provision, and that only Satan made him forget to mention it. He adds that the fish took its way into the sea in a remarkable manner. The commentators broadly agree on the core events: the fish, which was salted or cooked according to the reports, came back to life when touched by water, slipped into the sea, and the water parted over its path like an arch or a tunnel. This sign was meant to show Moses where he would meet al-Khidr, since the missing fish marked the place. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the fish's path turned to stone as it passed, while al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya stress the marvel of its restored life. On the meaning of the forgetting, opinions differ: Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that attributing the forgetting to both men refers in fact to Yusha' alone, whereas al-Razi holds that Satan preoccupied the attendant's mind. Al-Zamakhshari suggests that the word 'strange' may be Moses' own exclamation of wonder, while others take it as the attendant's description. The commentators present these readings side by side without deciding between them.

This passage tells how Moses, having learned that a righteous servant was at the meeting place of the two seas, told his attendant that the missing fish was the sign they had been seeking, so they turned back, following their own tracks until they reached the spot. The commentators agree that the sign was the loss of the fish, which slipped into the sea and made a passage for itself as the water parted above it. They differ on how this happened. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada report that the water became hard like a rock or ice, while al-Kalbi says the fish came back to life after Yusha' performed ablution from the spring of life, and Ibn Zayd describes a fish that had been partly eaten. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the attendant forgot to tell Moses, and that the forgetting is attributed to both of them in the language of the Arabs. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, followed by al-Qurtubi, identify the servant as al-Khidr; other views on the name of the attendant or the length of the hiqb are mentioned by al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya but do not bear directly on the meaning of this verse. The meaning most commentators adopt is that they returned by following their footprints, which the word qasasan conveys.

The commentators explain that Moses and his young companion Yusha ibn Nun found at the meeting place of the two seas a righteous servant of God, whom most identify as al-Khidr on the basis of authentic hadiths. God had given him a mercy from Himself and taught him a knowledge from His presence, which is called laduni knowledge. The commentators differ on his status. Most hold that he was a prophet, al-Baydawi and others specifying that he was not a messenger, while some describe him as a saint rather than a prophet, and Ibn Uthaymin inclines to the view that he was neither prophet nor messenger but a righteous servant granted miracles. On whether he is still alive, Ibn Kathir judges the hadiths that claim so to be weak, while later scholars such as Ibn al-Salah and al-Nawawi lean toward his survival, and Ibn al-Qayyim discusses the mystical traditions around him at length. Accounts also vary on his name and lineage. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that this knowledge should not be confused with ordinary prophetic revelation, and Ibn 'Ashur observes that Moses sought a particular kind of knowledge rather than a general law. The verse thus shows that God may grant some servants a knowledge particular to them, distinct from the outward law that Moses held.

This verse records Moses, peace be upon him, asking al-Khadir to accompany him and teach him, from what God has taught him, some right guidance (rushd), that is, knowledge that will lead him to what is correct. The commentators agree that this Moses is the son of Imran and that the righteous servant is al-Khadir according to the majority view. They stress the courtesy of the request: Moses asks permission to follow, admits his lack of knowledge, and seeks only part of what the other has. Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi argue that this does not lower a prophet's standing, since a messenger must be the most knowledgeable of his people in what he was sent with, not in everything, and a student may follow a teacher even when their ranks differ. Al-Zamakhshari cites the report of Said ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abbas to refute those who claimed this Moses was Moses son of Mitha; Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi likewise hold that he is the son of Imran. Abu Amr and Yaqub read 'rashadan' with two fathas, the others 'rushdan', which the scholars treat as two forms of the same word. Al-Razi lists many courtesies Moses shows: he makes himself a follower, asks leave, and confesses his ignorance. Al-Khadir replies that Moses will not be able to bear patience with him, since what he will see may appear objectionable, and Moses promises patience, adding 'if God wills'.

This verse records Khidr's reply to Moses: he will not be able to bear patiently with him, because what Khidr does appears outwardly objectionable, and Moses does not know its inner reality. The commentators agree on the setting: Moses asks to follow Khidr and learn some of the knowledge he has been taught, and Khidr answers with this warning before Moses promises, God willing, to be patient and obedient. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the patience meant is restraint from objecting or from asking questions. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the meaning covers both. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi stress that the learner follows the scholar even when their ranks differ. Al-Razi draws from the verse an argument that capacity does not exist before the act, while al-Jubba'i reads it as meaning only that patience would be burdensome for Moses. Al-Zamakhshari explains that a righteous man, let alone a prophet, cannot restrain his indignation at what seems wrong and rushes to object. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Biqa'i note that Khidr is warning Moses so that he may follow with open eyes. Ibn Kathir reports that Khidr has a knowledge God gave him that Moses lacks, while Moses is bound by the outward law. Several commentators see in these words a lesson on the humility of the student and the need for patience in learning.

This verse records the Khidr's words to Moses: how can you be patient with what you have not encompassed in knowledge? Commentators explain that the Khidr's actions appear objectionable outwardly, while their inner wisdom is beyond Moses' grasp, so he cannot endure them without knowing their reality. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi note that the Khidr possessed a hidden knowledge that Moses had not been given, while al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud argue that a righteous man, let alone a prophet, cannot restrain himself from condemning what seems wrong. They agree that 'khubran' is an accusative of specification or a verbal noun meaning 'not being informed of it'. Moses replies with a promise of patience and obedience, qualified by God's will. Al-Mawardi lists possible meanings of 'nor will I disobey your command': not beginning to object before the other speaks, or not divulging a secret. Ibn 'Ashur sees it as the student's duty to obey the teacher. Al-Razi draws from the verse that the ability to endure does not precede the act, a view disputed by al-Jubba'i, who reads it as a description of the burden of the task. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi also note that Moses' promise is conditional on God's will, and that he partly failed to keep it. Al-Sa'di emphasises that thorough understanding of a matter is the main foundation of patience.

This verse records Moses' promise to his teacher, al-Khidr: he says that Allah willing, he will find him patient with what he sees and will not disobey any of his commands. According to the commentators, Moses wanted to learn a knowledge that al-Khidr possessed and he did not, so he showed humility and submission. The reservation about God's will is read by many as a sign of courtesy towards God and an acknowledgment that patience and obedience come only through His help. Al-Khidr had earlier warned Moses that he would not be able to bear his actions, whose outward appearance seems objectionable while their hidden wisdom is beyond him. Exegetes generally see in the promise a readiness to learn with humility and docility.

The commentators differ on the grammar of the end of the verse. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi read "and I will not disobey any command of yours" as coordinated with "patient", so that the reservation covers both pledges; al-Alusi considers this the better reading. Al-Qurtubi notes that patience concerns the future while not disobeying is stated in the present, and so the reservation applies only to patience. Al-Razi draws theological points from the verse, including the question of the infallibility of prophets, which he answers by saying that the words of al-Khidr refer to the general case, and he discusses what an order implies. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari stress the concrete sense of obedience, while Ibn Ashur adds that the learner must accept the teacher's guidance on the points he is taught.

The commentators therefore draw from this verse the lesson of a student's patience and submission to his teacher, and that a promise about the future should be accompanied by a reservation regarding God's will.

Al-Khidr sets a condition before the journey begins: if Moses follows him, he must not ask about any deed until al-Khidr himself explains it. The commentators read the verse as teaching the student not to challenge or question the teacher ahead of time, but to wait until the teacher offers the explanation. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the phrase to mean until I begin to tell you about it myself, and al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu al-Su'ud draw the same lesson of conduct. All agree that this condition belongs to the etiquette of the student towards the teacher and of the follower towards the one he follows. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi add that the student may feel displeasure at something he does not understand, yet should hold back until it is explained. The main disagreement concerns recitation: Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read the verb with a doubled nun, while the others read it without doubling, and Ibn 'Atiyya notes that these readings are close in meaning. Several scholars add that the teacher may reasonably delay the explanation when the student is not yet ready to understand it. Al-Razi draws lessons from the passage about the student's humility, without judging between the readings or the interpretations.

According to the commentators, Moses and al-Khidr boarded a ship whose crew had carried them without charging a fare. Once the vessel had reached the open sea, al-Khidr pulled one or two planks from the side facing the water. Moses reproached him: have you pierced it so as to drown its people? You have done a monstrous thing. Lexicographers cited by the tafsirs explain that imr means something grave and alarming. The commentators agree that Moses objected to what looked like an obvious wrong, and that al-Khidr reminded him of his promise not to be impatient, while Moses excused himself by forgetfulness. Al-Tabari and al-Mawardi explain that the objection concerned the danger of drowning. Al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir hold that the lam in li-tughriqa marks consequence rather than purpose. On the reading, most readers have tu-ughriqa with ahlaha in the accusative, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read yaghraqa with ahlu-ha in the nominative; al-Tabari judges both readings equivalent in meaning. On the meaning of imran, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir report three views: reprehensible, according to Mujahid; astonishing, according to Qatada and Ibn Qutayba; and calamitous, according to Abu 'Ubayda. Some reports say Ibn 'Abbas related that Moses stepped aside after the ship was damaged, before al-Khidr revealed what he had been thinking. Abu Yusuf drew from the passage a permission for a guardian to diminish an orphan's property when this serves his interest, but most commentators do not address that question.

This verse records the servant of God, usually identified with al-Khadir, reminding Moses that he would not be able to bear patiently being in his company. The commentators explain that Moses had objected to actions that looked wrong without knowing their wisdom, so the reminder refers back to the condition they had agreed upon. The commentators differ on Moses' words, "do not hold me to account for what I forgot." Ibn Abbas and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, as transmitted by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, held that he did not really forget but spoke in an indirect manner (ma'arid al-kalam). Al-Tabari in one of his views, and Ibn al-Jawzi, took forgetting to mean abandoning, that is failing to keep the promise. Most exegetes, including al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi, take forgetting in its literal sense, relying on the authentic hadith that calls Moses' first lapse a forgetting. The plea "do not burden me with a difficult matter" means not to impose hardship on him or make his companionship oppressive, and the commentators agree on this general sense. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi note that the reminder comes before the reproach, and that Moses apologises to get out of the situation. Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan think Moses had truly forgotten his undertaking, since the deeds looked objectionable. Others hold that the verse allows several readings. The common lesson is that bearing what one does not understand is difficult, and that the excuse of forgetting is accepted, according to the commentators.

The verse records Moses' plea to the wise servant (al-Khidr) after his objection: « Do not hold me to account for what I forgot », meaning do not penalize me for failing to keep your condition, and « do not burden me with difficulty in my affair », meaning do not make it hard for me to follow you or make my companionship too strained. The commentators agree that Moses asks for leniency and ease in this companionship, but they differ on the meaning of forgetting. Ibn Abbas, in one transmission, and Ubayy ibn Ka'b held that Moses did not truly forget; he spoke in indirect language, a device used to avoid lying while achieving his aim. The majority, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Atiyya, held that he really forgot the covenant, relying on the hadith: « The first time was forgetfulness on Moses' part ». Ibn Abbas, in another transmission, explained the sense as 'what you left of your covenant'. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya combined both readings: Moses framed his words as a plea not to be blamed for forgetting, in order to widen his excuse. As for the word 'turhiqni', al-Farra' took it to mean 'do not hurry me', Abu 'Ubayda and al-Zajjaj took it to mean 'do not cover me', and Ibn al-Jawzi took it to mean 'do not burden me'. All agree on the meaning: deal with me gently rather than harshly. A variant reading 'usuran' with two vowels is also transmitted, and the commentators draw no ruling from it.

This verse describes how, after they left the boat, Moses and al-Khidr walked along the shore and met a young boy whom al-Khidr killed. Moses protested that he had slain a pure soul who had done nothing to deserve death, and called the act a grave wrong. The commentators agree that it was a killing, but they differ on the boy's age. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and most scholars, as Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir report, held that he had not reached puberty, while al-Hasan and Ibn 'Atiyya said he was a grown man, since Arabs sometimes call a young man a boy. On the meaning of "zakiyya", al-Tabari, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take it as pure, repentant or Muslim, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' distinguishes the one who never sinned from the one who sinned and then repented, and Abu 'Ubayda distinguishes bodily purity from purity of religion. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' regard the two readings as having the same meaning. On which act was worse, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that this second act was more heinous than the first, while others argue the first was graver because it endangered the whole crew, and a life, once lost, cannot be restored. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi note that Moses objected before understanding the reason, and al-Qurtubi draws from the phrase "without a life taken" the principle of retaliation.

This verse records the rebuke of al-Khadir to Moses when Moses again objects, this time to the killing of the young boy. He reminds Moses that he will not be able to bear patience with him, and adds the word "lak" (to you) to intensify the rebuke, since the disobedience was repeated after a first warning. The commentators agree that Moses then commits himself to ask no more questions, and that if he does so again they must part, for al-Khadir will then have been sufficiently excused. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Attiyya cite hadiths on this point, but Abu Hayyan notes that only the Prophet's own words are relied upon: the first objection was forgetfulness. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain the added "lak" as a sign of stronger reproach. Al-Mawardi gives several senses of "fala tusahibni": do not follow me, do not keep company with me, do not help me. Al-Tabari prefers the reading with the doubled nun in "ladunni" as the best known, while Ibn Attiyya records the variant readings. The phrase "qad balagta min ladunni 'udhran" means that al-Khadir has given Moses a sufficient excuse for parting. Ibn Ashur sees in this wording a way of sparing his companion embarrassment at being refused. Ibn Kathir adds that al-Khadir had warned Moses several times. Ibn 'Uthaymin observes that the "lak" makes this rebuke stronger than the first. The general meaning is therefore a reminder to be patient and faithful to the commitment made, with parting if the promise is broken.

The commentators explain that Moses, after being warned by al-Khidr that he would not be able to bear patience with him, says that if he asks him about anything again, he should part from him, for he has been given a sufficient excuse on his part. Most read "from my side" as "from me". Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir cite the hadith in which the Prophet said: "May God have mercy on Moses; had he been patient he would have seen the wonder", and they explain that Moses was overcome with shame before his companion. On the readings, al-Tabari preferred the doubled-nun form "ladunni" as the more widely known, while holding all the recognised readings to be valid. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take "balaghta" to mean that the excuse has been reached and become complete. The commentators agree on the core point: Moses accepts separation at a third objection, and al-Khidr acknowledges that the excuse was given across two violations. The verse thus combines Moses's deep regret with his respect for his teacher.

The verse tells how Moses and his companion, al-Khidr, reached a town and asked its people for food, meaning the hospitality owed to travellers, but they refused to host them. There they found a wall leaning and about to collapse, and al-Khidr set it upright. Moses then said that had he wished, he could have taken a payment for the work, since they had been denied hospitality. The commentators agree that the townspeople were at fault in refusing, and that attributing a wish to the wall is a figure of speech meaning it was on the point of falling; al-Tabari and others consider the matter open, allowing that God may have given it a real intention. On the name of the town, Ibn Abbas and Qatada said Antioch, Ibn Sirin said al-Ubulla, while others mentioned Barqa, Bajarwan or places in al-Andalus, and several scholars regarded the disagreement as unresolved by any reliable report. On how the wall was straightened, Sa'id ibn Jubayr said al-Khidr touched it with his hand and it stood, Ibn Abbas said he pulled it down and rebuilt it, and some mention propping it with a pillar. Some readers vowel the verb as lattakhadhta, and others as latakhidta, but the meaning remains taking. Moses's remark is understood as a reproach for not asking for pay, given their need for food. Several draw from this that asking for food when in need is permissible and that hospitality is a praiseworthy duty, though scholars differ on whether it is obligatory.

The Khidr tells Moses that this is the parting between them and that he will now explain the meaning of the deeds Moses could not bear to witness in silence. The commentators agree that the word "this" refers either to the parting promised by Moses's words "do not keep company with me," to the third objection that caused the separation, or simply to the present moment. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Nasafi explain that the original phrasing was "a separation between me and you," with the verbal noun attached to the adverbial phrase by extension; Ibn Abi 'Abla also read it that way. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan see the repetition of "between" as emphasis. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi take "ta'wil" to mean the outcome or end toward which the deeds lead. Al-Razi lists the three purposes: saving the boat from a king who seized every sound vessel, saving the parents of the boy and giving them a better child, and preserving the treasure for the orphans. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the relative clause gently reproaches Moses for his haste and lack of patience. On the Khidr's status, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani report that most scholars hold him to be a prophet, while Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Ashur regard him as a righteous servant, Ibn 'Ashur leaning toward prophethood with caution. The verse itself offers no further detail on the question.

In this verse al-Khidr explains to Musa why he damaged the boat. He says its owners were poor people who earned their living on the sea, and that a king was waiting behind them to seize every sound boat. So he wanted to make it defective, so that the king would leave it and it would remain with its owners. The commentators agree on this core meaning: the damage was meant to turn the usurper away. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi hold this reading. The word masakin has several explanations. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi list meanings such as poverty, weakness or chronic illness. Ka'b said the owners were ten brothers, five of them disabled and five working at sea, a report repeated by al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Atiyya notes that most readers use the unstressed form, while the stressed reading was taken to mean sailors or tanners. On the phrase wara'ahum, Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Abu Ubayda, al-Zajjaj and Ibn Atiyya take it to mean in front of them, while others take it to mean behind them, since the owners would return past the king. Al-Tabari mentions the view that the word is an antonym, but does not accept it, and Ibn Atiyya holds that it keeps its ordinary sense in terms of time. The name of the king is also disputed, with Hudad ibn Budad and Jalandi among the names given, and no name is firmly established. Finally, the commentators differ on whether kulla safina means every boat or only sound ones. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take it as sound boats, and al-Shinqiti explains that the restriction follows from the purpose of the damage.

The commentators explain that al-Khidr killed the boy because God revealed to him that, if he grew up, he would drive his two believing parents into rebellion and disbelief, either through their excessive love for him or their need of him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the verb khashina means for many scholars 'we knew', while others read it as 'we disliked'; Ibn Atiyya treats the reading 'fa-khafa rabbuka' in Ibn Mas'ud's codex as a metaphor. On the boy's condition, al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir rely on the report from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he was born disbelieving, whereas al-Qurtubi, al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud consider whether he was a discerning child or a young man who committed robbery and corruption. As for the replacement the parents received, most mention a daughter who bore a prophet, others a righteous Muslim son, and some seventy prophets, a view Ibn Atiyya finds unlikely. The recitations differ between yubaddilahuma with shadda or without, and ruhman with a sukun or damma on the ha', which commentators regard as variants of nearly the same meaning. Several, including Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn 'Ashur, draw from the story the principle of accepting a lesser harm to avert a greater one, and all agree that the act rested on a divine command.

The Khidr explains to Moses why he killed the young boy: had he grown up, he would have pressed his believing parents into transgression and disbelief. God therefore willed to give them in his place a child better in purity and piety and closer to them in compassion. The readers differ on the verb form: Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read it with doubling, the others without, and al-Tabari judges the two readings close in meaning. Ibn 'Abbas took zakat to mean religion, Ibn 'Atiyya uprightness and virtue, and al-Zamakhshari freedom from sin. For ruhm, Qatada understood dutiful kindness to parents, Ibn Jurayj compassion towards them, and al-Farra' that they would feel more tenderness towards the new child. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, report that God gave them a daughter who bore a prophet, and some add that she bore seventy prophets, a figure Ibn 'Atiyya considers far-fetched. Several scholars, including al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan, discuss who speaks the phrase "we feared", attributing it either to the Khidr or to God, and explain the verb as knowledge, fear or dislike.

Al-Khidr explains to Moses the reason for his act regarding the wall: it belonged to two orphan boys in the town, and beneath it lay a buried treasure that was theirs, and their father had been righteous.
