God willed that they reach maturity and recover their treasure as a mercy from their Lord, and he says he did not act on his own opinion but by God's command. The commentators differ on the treasure: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say it was pages of knowledge, while Ikrima and Qatada say it was wealth, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir prefer the meaning of buried money, which best fits the wording of the verse. Some report, through chains mostly judged weak, a golden tablet carrying wise sayings. On the righteous father, some say he was their immediate father, others his seventh or tenth ancestor, and Ibn 'Abbas adds that the boys were protected by their father's piety. As for whether al-Khidr is still alive, most exegetes, including al-Bukhari and Ibn Kathir, hold that he has died, while others maintain he lives on. All agree the act was based on divine revelation, and al-Razi draws lessons from it about providence. The verse teaches that an apparent harm may hide a mercy, and that people often do not grasp the wisdom of an event until it is disclosed to them.

This verse records the question that the polytheists, prompted by the Jews, put to the Prophet about Dhu al-Qarnayn. God tells him to answer that he will recite to them a part of his story as a reminder. The commentators explain that God established him on earth and gave him a way to every thing, that is knowledge and means. He followed these means to the west, where he saw the sun set in a murky spring, and found a people there whom God allowed him to punish or treat kindly. He chose to call them to faith: whoever does wrong will be punished, while whoever believes and acts righteously will receive a good reward and gentle words. He then reached the east, and then the place between the two barriers. The commentators agree that he was a righteous and just king, and that the means granted to him are not detailed. They differ on his identity. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and others identify him with Alexander the Macedonian, though Ibn Kathir holds that an earlier Alexander lived in the time of Abraham. Al-Biruni saw him as a king of Himyar, others as the Persian king Fereydun, and Ibn Ashur as a Chinese ruler. They also differ on whether he was a prophet: some held him to be one, while Ali ibn Abi Talib and many others considered him a righteous servant, neither prophet nor king, and others a just king. As for his title, the explanations vary: he reached the two horns of the sun, he had two braids, or he was struck on the head twice for calling people to God. All draw from the story a lesson on justice, piety, and the power God grants to whom He wills.

The commentators explain that God states He established Dhu al-Qarnayn firmly on earth, meaning He gave him authority and the ability to act in it, and gave him a means (sabab) to reach whatever he sought from every matter. For most, these means are knowledge, power and equipment, as well as the paths of conquest and victory over enemies. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak take sabab to mean knowledge, al-Hasan takes it as the means of arriving wherever he wished, and Mujahid as a road or a stage of travel. Al-Tabari stresses that conquest and travel were accomplished through these means. Several reports say Dhu al-Qarnayn ruled the earth from east to west, and Mujahid counts among those who ruled the whole earth two believers, Solomon and Dhu al-Qarnayn, and two unbelievers, Nimrod and Nebuchadnezzar.

On his identity opinions differ. Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Kathir do not identify him with Alexander the Macedonian, whereas al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take him to be Alexander, while al-Shawkani and Ibn 'Ashur report other views, such as a Himyarite king or a Persian king. On his prophethood, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib says he was a righteous servant, neither prophet nor king, while Ibn 'Amr and al-Dahhak hold him to be a prophet and others regard him as a king. Some link the tamkin and the asbab to royal power, others to prophecy and miracles, and the commentators do not settle the matter. Al-Zamakhshari notes that God does not detail his means, so it is better to stop at what is reported. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di caution against the narratives taken from the Israelite traditions, which they consider unreliable.

The commentators explain that Dhu al-Qarnayn, about whom the polytheists asked the Prophet at the urging of the Jews, used the means God had given him and travelled across the earth to reach his goal, taking one route after another and one stage after another. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, prefer the wasla reading fa-ittaba'a in the sense of he travelled and proceeded. Al-Zajjaj, Abu Hayyan and al-Nasafi distinguish the two forms and take atba'a to mean he caught up with, while Ibn 'Atiyya considers that both senses may be intended. Most commentators understand sabab as a route or a stage, though Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by al-Tabari, also takes it to mean knowledge that God had given him.

On the identity of Dhu al-Qarnayn, opinions differ widely. Many identify him with Alexander, while Ibn Kathir and al-Suhayli maintain that there were two different men, and others say he was a pious servant or a Yemeni king. The commentators also disagree about why he was called Dhu al-Qarnayn, offering several explanations, such as two tresses of hair or his reaching both ends of the earth. Whether he was a prophet or a king is likewise a matter on which they differ.

The commentators explain that this verse describes Dhu al-Qarnayn's journey to the furthest west, where he saw the sun seem to set in a spring, found a people beside it, and was given the choice between punishing them and dealing kindly with them. Most agree that punishment means execution if they persist in disbelief, and that kindness means calling them to faith and teaching them the law, or taking them captive after victory. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that Ka'b al-Ahbar, when asked, said the Torah describes the sun setting in mud, matching Ibn 'Abbas's reading. Al-Tabari judges both readings, 'muddy' (hami'a) and 'hot' (hamiya), to be valid, since the spring may be both hot and muddy, and Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya accept this reconciliation. Al-Razi, following Abu Ali al-Jubba'i, explains that the setting in the spring is a visual appearance, like a sailor who sees the sun sink into the sea. On Dhu al-Qarnayn's prophethood, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi argue that he was a prophet, while Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir incline to inspiration or revelation transmitted through a prophet, without a firm conclusion. Abu Hayyan and al-Baydawi note that the wording highlights kindness as the preferred option.

The commentators explain that this verse is part of Dhu al-Qarnayn's answer to a people he met at the setting place of the sun. God had given him the choice between punishing them or treating them kindly, and he decided to punish whoever persists in wrongdoing, which most of them take to mean associating partners with God. Such a person will be put to death in this world and then punished in the Hereafter with a dreadful punishment. As for whoever believes and does righteous deeds, he will receive a good reward and will be spoken to gently and given ease. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that the wrongdoing means disbelief and polytheism, and that al-husna means Paradise or the good deeds. The recitations differ on the word jaza'an: the people of Madina, Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read it in the construct form, while Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read it in the accusative with tanwin. Al-Tabari prefers the accusative, treating it as a verbal complement, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya and others explain that the construct form makes Paradise itself the reward. As for the nature of the punishment, most describe it as severe and unprecedented, while Ibn 'Uthaymin says the strangeness lies in how the punished person perceives it. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the killing is the worldly punishment, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi leave its nature open. Ibn Kathir warns that some of the accounts come from Israelite traditions. The commentators present these different views without judging between them.

This verse concludes the account of Dhu al-Qarnayn by setting the reward of those who believe and do righteous deeds against the punishment of the one who persists in wrongdoing. Most commentators understand the "good reward" (al-husna) as Paradise: al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and others take it this way, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Qasimi allow that it may refer to the good deed itself, especially the testimony of faith. As for "ease from Our command", al-Tabari explains that God teaches him what brings him closer to Him and softens his speech, citing Mujahid who said it means kindness. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir read it as dealing gently with him, whereas al-Razi and al-Baydawi take it as an order that is easy and not burdensome, such as zakat or land tax. Ibn Atiyya notes that all actions come from God's creation, which is why ease is attributed to speech.

Readers differ on the grammar of "reward". Al-Tabari prefers the accusative with tanwin, reading the reward as an explanation of the good, while the majority of readers from Medina, Basra and Kufa read it in the construct form. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy mention other grammatical options, such as an accusative of manner or a circumstantial clause. Ibn Ashur stresses that the verse contrasts the punishment of the polytheist with the reward of the one who believes after being given the choice, since the believer is one who has turned away from disbelief.

The commentators explain that Dhu al-Qarnayn, having reached the setting place of the sun, took another route, pursuing the means God had given him, until he reached the rising place of the sun. There he found a people whom God had not shielded from the sun by any covering: their land could not bear buildings and had neither mountains nor trees. When the sun rose they hid in burrows or in water, and came out to their livelihoods after it had passed its zenith. The exegetes agree that the verse expresses how close the sun was to these people and how fully exposed they were to it, and that God encompassed in knowledge all that was with Dhu al-Qarnayn.

Al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Kathir report that they lived in a land where no building could stand, and al-Hasan and Ibn Juraij add that they moved about like animals, and that an army once died there when the sun rose on it. Qatada identifies them with the Zanj, while Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi record other identifications. Al-Razi understands that, like the peoples of equatorial regions, they went unclothed, and al-Zamakhshari notes that the word for covering can also mean clothing.

Opinions differ on the word "kadhalika". Al-Tabari links it to the pursuit of the route, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya see it as an expression of the greatness of Dhu al-Qarnayn's affair, while al-Baydawi and al-Alusi take it as a comparison between this people and those at the sunset. Al-Shawkani notes that the exegetes have debated at length who Dhu al-Qarnayn actually was, and do not reach a decisive conclusion among the various identifications.

This verse describes Dhu al-Qarnayn reaching the far east, where he finds the sun rising over a people who had no shelter from it. The commentators broadly agree on the plain meaning: their land could not support buildings, and they had no trees, mountains or other cover. When the sun rose they hid in caves or in the water, and came out to their livelihoods once it had risen high. Al-Hasan and Qatada report that they came out like grazing animals, and Ibn Jurayj adds that no building was ever erected there.

Scholars differ on who these people were. Qatada says they were the Zanj, al-Zamakhshari also notes this view, and Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir record other opinions. Ibn Atiyya mentions India and the lands beyond it, and Kalbi describes them as naked and barefoot. The meaning of "a covering" is also debated. Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi take it as an image of the sun's closeness and its effect on them, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir also understand it as clothing, and Mujahid reports that most black people do not wear clothes at sunrise.

On the word "thus", al-Tabari reads it as meaning that Dhu al-Qarnayn reached the east just as he had reached the west, while al-Baydawi and al-Razi offer several readings, including that he judged them as he had judged the people of the west. The phrase "and We encompassed what was with him in knowledge" is explained by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd as knowledge, and by al-Zamakhshari as a reference to the abundance of his troops and resources.

The commentators explain that this verse continues the account of Dhu al-Qarnayn's journey eastward. He reached the farthest inhabited place in the east and found the sun rising over a people with no shelter against it, neither building, tree, nor clothing. Most read this as a land where no structures could stand: al-Tabari, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Jurayj report that these people took refuge in underground galleries or in water when the sun was up, and came out to seek food when it had passed. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari take the 'screen' more broadly as the scorching nearness of the sun, and al-Zamakhshari also mentions that they went naked. On the identity of the people there is disagreement: Qatada names them the Zanj, Ibn Kathir follows him, while al-Mawardi and others cite older names and say such reports are not verified. Scholars also differ on the word 'kadhalika': al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya relate it to his conduct, which was the same as in the west; al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi read it as the same judgment applied to these people as to those of the west, choosing punishment or kindness; al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud link it to the greatness of his power and rule. On the closing phrase, the commentators agree that God knows fully what is with Dhu al-Qarnayn, his troops and his means. Ibn Kathir and al-Suyuti render it as knowledge, while al-Zamakhshari reads it as a stress on the vastness of his forces, and al-Razi notes that the verse highlights God's complete awareness of all his affairs.

The commentators explain that this verse opens Dhu al-Qarnayn's third journey, in which he took a new path crossing between east and west, following the means God had granted him. Most read the word sabab as a route or a stage leading to his goal. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that he reached a place between two barriers, two mountains that he closed off with a rampart. They differ on where these lie: Ibn Abbas, al-Tabari and al-Baydawi place them between Armenia and Azerbaijan, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya locate them at the eastern edge of Turkish lands, Ibn Atiyya admitting he cannot confirm this. On the vowelling of the word sadd, al-Kisa'i holds that the two forms mean the same thing, whereas Ikrima, Abu Amr ibn al-Ala and Abu Ubayda distinguish between what comes from God and what is made by people. All agree that the people found beyond the barriers could barely understand speech. Some identify them as Turks, though the commentators do not all agree on their precise identity.

The verse describes how Dhu al-Qarnayn, after reaching the place of sunset, followed another route until he came to a place between two mountains, where he found beyond them a people who could barely understand any speech and could only be understood with difficulty and slowness. The commentators agree that the two barriers are two mountains with a gap between them through which harm would come. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi place the mountains between Armenia and Azerbaijan or at the edge of Turkish lands, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi locate them further north, and Abu Hayyan gives no firm location. On the reading of the two forms of the word meaning barrier, al-Kisa'i holds they are two dialects with the same meaning, while Ikrima and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' distinguish them by whether the barrier is God's creation or human work; al-Tabari judges both readings correct. As for Gog and Magog, most say they are two peoples descended from Adam or from Japheth son of Noah, some identify them with the Turks, and al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi note that their name may derive from a root meaning to blaze or to mix. On their corruption, Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz says it was eating human beings, others say killing and oppression, and al-Tabari holds it was a feared future harm rather than past wrongdoing. The word kharj is, according to Abu 'Amr, a gift given once, while kharaj is a recurring tax; Ibn 'Abbas understood it as a payment. Dhu al-Qarnayn declines the payment, saying what God has granted him is better, and asks for help with strength and labour to build a barrier called radm. The commentators also relate many accounts about these peoples and about Dhu al-Qarnayn's identity, which many judge unreliable, as Ibn Kathir notes.

This passage tells how people living between two mountains, who barely understand foreign speech, ask Dhu al-Qarnayn to build a barrier against Yajuj and Majuj, who spread corruption among them, and offer him payment for the work. The commentators agree that Yajuj and Majuj are two peoples descended from Adam, and that their corruption includes killing, plundering and destroying crops. They differ on whether this corruption had already happened: Ibn Abbas and others hold that it had, while al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Atiyya read it as corruption still to come when they emerge. Most readers say kharjan, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i say kharajan; al-Tabari links it to tribute or revenue, and Abu 'Amr distinguishes the kharj, a voluntary gift, from the kharaj, a fixed due. Dhu al-Qarnayn declines the payment, saying what God has given him is better, and asks for their physical help and for iron blocks and molten copper. The location of the two mountains is disputed: between Armenia and Azerbaijan according to Ibn Abbas, or at the far edge of Turkish lands to the east according to others. On the vowelling of sadd, al-Kisa'i holds the two forms to be dialect variants with one meaning, while 'Ikrima distinguishes what humans made, with a, from what God made, with u.

This passage of the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn describes a people who barely understood other languages complaining to him about the corruption of Gog and Magog in their land, and offering him money to build a barrier between them. He replied that what God had granted him of power and wealth was better than their offer, and asked them to help him with strength, meaning workers, craftsmen and tools, so that he could build a solid rampart between them. The commentators agree that the radm is stronger and more solid than the sadd, a word taken from patching a garment layer upon layer. al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya explain the strength as men and labourers, al-Kalbi as tools, and al-Zamakhshari combines the two, speaking of craftsmen and instruments. Ibn 'Abbas and others take the radm to mean the strongest barrier. The readers differ over the vocalisation of «sadd»: al-Kisa'i holds that the two forms are dialects with one meaning, whereas Abu 'Ubayda, al-Khalil and Sibawayh distinguish the noun from the verbal noun, and 'Ikrima and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' distinguish what is God's creation from what is human work. The commentators explain that Gog and Magog are two peoples descended from Adam or from Yafith, and that their emergence is among the signs of the Hour. The verse contains few legal rulings, apart from the permissibility of paying for labour and the merit of offering effort freely.

The verse describes Dhu al-Qarnayn asking his people to bring him blocks of iron. When he had piled them between the two mountains, he ordered them to light a fire until the iron glowed like fire, and then to pour molten copper over it so that it fused into a solid mass. The commentators generally agree that zubar means pieces or blocks of iron, and that the two sadafayn are the two sides of the mountains facing each other. On the word qitr, most read it as molten copper, while Abu Ubayda took it to mean molten iron and Ibn al-Anbari said molten lead. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the structure was a barrier against Gog and Magog, built with alternating layers of iron, wood and charcoal. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi note that the different readings of sadafayn carry the same meaning. Regarding the statement that they could neither scale the barrier nor breach it, the commentators explain that it was too high and smooth to climb and too solid to dig through. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Abu Hurayra about the people digging through it each day, but notes its wording raises doubts. The phrase about the barrier becoming level ground at the appointed time is read by all as referring to the Day of Resurrection or the time of the people's emergence. Scholars disagree about the location of the barrier: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir place it between Armenia and Azerbaijan, al-Razi leans toward the north, and Ibn Ashur places it northwest of the Gobi desert.

The commentators explain that this verse describes how Gog and Magog were unable to get past the barrier built by Dhul-Qarnayn: they could neither climb over it, because it was high and smooth, nor break through it from below, because it was solid and thick. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the zubar al-hadid as pieces of iron, and the qitr as molten copper, though al-Bahr al-Muhit and others note that some scholars took it to mean molten lead or molten iron. Most agree that the pronoun in "yazharuhu" refers to the barrier and that the verb means to scale it, while Qatada is cited as saying that the breach would be made at its base. Grammarians such as al-Farra and Abu Ali treat the dropped ta' in "fa-ma ista'u" as a light form, and regard Hamza's assimilated reading as weak. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report the hadith of Abu Hurayra about the daily digging and the wall's repair, but Ibn Kathir considers its wording problematic and suspects it goes back to Ka'b al-Ahbar. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi take "this is a mercy from my Lord" to refer to the barrier, while others read it as referring to the power to build it. The promise of God is generally taken to mean the approach of the Hour, or the appointed time of their emergence, when the barrier will be levelled.

Dhul-Qarnayn says that this barrier is a mercy from his Lord, and that when the promise of his Lord comes, He will level it to the ground, for the promise of his Lord is true. The commentators read this verse as the closing words of the story of Dhul-Qarnayn, after he built the iron and molten copper barrier that stopped Gog and Magog from crossing or breaching it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi agree that the promise refers to the emergence of Gog and Magog, and that the verb means to level. They cite the report of Abu Hurayra about their digging at the wall each day, which God restores each time. Ibn Kathir finds its chain sound but its wording doubtful and thinks it goes back to Ka'b al-Ahbar. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Ashur take the promise to mean the approach of the Day of Resurrection. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya leave both meanings open. The readings differ between the masculine accusative 'dakkan' and 'dakka'', with a long alif, which compares the wall to a camel with no hump. The general lesson shared by the commentaries is that every human barrier remains subject to God's will.

This part of the verse describes what will happen at the end of time, when the barrier built by Dhu al-Qarnayn is levelled and God's promise comes true. The commentators read the phrase "surging into one another" as agitation and mingling. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari take the pronoun to refer to Gog and Magog, who push against each other as they pour out from behind the barrier and spread across the land. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi also allow that it refers to all creatures on the Day of Resurrection, when humans and jinn become bewildered and mix together. Ibn 'Atiyya prefers to read the whole passage as concerning the Last Day. All agree that the trumpet is the blast of resurrection, sounded by Israfil, and that the Sur is a horn, with several reports from the Prophet describing the blasts of alarm, of death and of rising. God then gathers all creation for judgement.

The commentators then describe the state of the disbelievers to whom Hell is displayed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di explain that their eyes were veiled from the remembrance of God, meaning the Qur'an and the signs, and that they could not bear to listen to the truth, either out of hostility or because wretchedness had overcome them. Al-Razi notes that this inability to hear is stronger than deafness, since a deaf person may hear when shouted at. Commentators differ on the sense of "presenting" Hell: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as a real display of the fire, while Ibn 'Ashur sees a mocking tone in it.

Taken together, these explanations affirm resurrection and recompense, the point on which most commentators agree.

The commentators explain that this verse describes what will happen on the Day of Resurrection: Hell will be brought forth and displayed to the disbelievers so that they see it with their own eyes before entering it, which adds to their distress. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi, agree that the word means making it manifest and visible, that the display is real rather than figurative, and that it concerns the disbelievers in particular because it is for their sake. Al-Tabari supports this with a line of poetry by 'Amr ibn Kulthum and reports that Hell will appear to them like a mirage. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir stress the purpose of intensifying fear and warning.

The commentators also agree that the phrase "whose eyes were veiled from My remembrance" describes their turning away from the signs of God, their heedlessness and their refusal. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi take the blindness to be a blindness of the heart and insight. Al-Razi holds that the blindness and deafness mentioned show extreme refusal, and that their state is worse than deafness, since a deaf person may hear when called loudly. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that being unable to hear means being unwilling to accept, out of deep aversion.

There is disagreement about when this display occurs. Al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya link it to the emergence of Gog and Magog, while al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan place it on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the word means a real exposure, whereas Ibn 'Ashur sees it as a way to make listeners grasp the reality of the resurrection.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the disbelievers to whom Hell will be displayed on the Day of Resurrection. Saying that their eyes were under a covering from the Reminder means that they did not reflect on God's signs or benefit from them. As for the phrase they could not hear, Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di take it as deliberate refusal and turning away from guidance, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi note that it is stronger than simply calling them deaf, since a deaf person may still hear when shouted at, whereas these people seem to have had their ears stopped up. Mujahid understands hearing here as understanding, while Ibn 'Abbas and al-Baghawi understand it as the hearing of acceptance and faith, given that wretchedness had overcome them, and al-Baghawi also reports that they could not listen to the Prophet because of their intense hostility. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes between the covering over the vision of God's signs and the covering over understanding the Qur'an, saying that the covering begins in the heart before spreading to the eyes. On the word nuzul, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi take it as a dwelling place, whereas others take it as what is prepared for a guest, which would be an ironic image. The scholars therefore agree on the meaning of turning away from the truth, and their differences concern how to understand the covering and the hearing.

The commentators explain that the verse is a rhetorical question of rebuke: do the disbelievers suppose that taking as protectors, besides God, His servants such as the angels, Jesus or Uzayr will benefit them or save them from punishment? They differ on who the servants are. Ibn Abbas says they are the devils the disbelievers obeyed, Muqatil says they are the idols, while the majority, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi, identify them as the angels, Jesus, Uzayr and all other objects of worship. The second part, "We have prepared Hell for the disbelievers as a nuzul", is read by Ibn Abbas and Qatada as an abode or food, by al-Zajjaj as a dwelling place, and by Ibn Qutayba as what is prepared for a guest, which makes it a mockery of them. All agree that the question denies that such alliances would benefit them. On recitation, most read "afahasiba" with a kasra, meaning "supposed", while Ali, Ikrima and Mujahid read "afahasbu" with a sukun, meaning "is it enough for them". Al-Zamakhshari considers the second reading well-founded, and al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan judge that both readings are valid.

God commands His Prophet to ask a warning question: shall we tell you who are the greatest losers in their deeds? The verse answers that they are those whose effort went astray in the life of this world while they thought they were doing good. The commentators agree that the verse covers anyone who acts on what he believes to be right while being wrong, and is not limited to one group. On who is meant, opinions differ. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report from Ali ibn Abi Talib and others that they are the monks who shut themselves in monasteries, and Ibn Kathir also reports that they are the Kharijites (Harurites). Al-Bukhari reports from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas that they are the Jews and Christians, and Ibn Abbas agrees. Ibn 'Atiyya argues that the verse refers to the pagan Arabs, since denying the meeting with God describes them, and al-Alusi and al-Shawkani cite similar views. Al-Tabari prefers the general reading, a position shared by Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Shinqiti, who hold that the wording's generality matters more than the specific occasion. Al-Baydawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that denying God's signs and the meeting with Him voids their deeds, so no scale will be set up for them on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir adds that their scales are empty of good. Al-Mawardi offers two meanings of not weighing: no good deeds to weigh, or no value and rank. The verse ends with their punishment in Hell for their disbelief and for mocking God's signs and messengers.

This verse speaks of those whose effort went astray in the life of this world while they thought they were doing good, and it calls them the greatest losers in deeds. The commentators differ on who they are. Al-Tabari concludes that the verse covers anyone who acts on a mistaken belief, whether from the People of the Book or not, a view followed by Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi. Others, citing 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, identify them as the monks who withdrew into monasteries, or as the Kharijites of Harura; Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Ibn 'Abbas name the Jews and Christians, and Mujahid says the People of the Book in general. Al-Qurtubi also reports Ibn 'Abbas saying they are the disbelievers of Mecca.

All agree that the effort's going astray means that it was wasted and brought no benefit. The following verses explain that these people denied the signs of their Lord and the meeting with Him, so their deeds are annulled. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that this is why no weight will be set up for them on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi offer two readings of the weight: either the scale is only for the deeds of believers, or such people have no worth in God's sight. The hadith of the large, heavy man who does not weigh a gnat's wing, recorded by al-Bukhari, is cited by Ibn Kathir and others.

The verses on the Gardens of Firdaws are explained by Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir as the highest part of Paradise, and its people will not desire any change from it.

The commentators explain that this verse describes those who denied the signs of God that testify to His oneness and to the truth of His messengers, and who denied meeting Him in the hereafter. Their deeds are therefore void and bring them no reward, and on the Day of Resurrection no scale will be set up for them, meaning they will have no weight or standing before God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand that their scales will not grow heavy for lack of good deeds, and they cite the hadith of Abu Hurayra about the corpulent man who will not weigh the wing of a mosquito. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi stress instead the contempt and disdain shown toward them, and al-Razi adds that no scale is set up at all for those whose sins outweigh their good. Ibn 'Atiyya also suggests that there may be no good deed to weigh, or that the phrase is a metaphor meaning they have no value. The early authorities differ on who the "greatest losers in deeds" of the preceding verse are: Ali and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas named monks, Jews and Christians, or the Kharijites of Harura, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir read the verse more broadly, covering anyone who worships God in a way He does not accept while thinking himself correct. Al-Razi explains that the Mu'tazilites cite this verse in support of the doctrine that disbelief cancels good deeds. As for the readings, "fa-la yuqimu" in the third person is reported from Mujahid and Ubayd ibn Umayr.

This passage, as the commentators read it, states that those who disbelieved in God's signs and in meeting Him will see their deeds rendered void, so that they carry no weight on the Day of Resurrection, and that their recompense is Hell for their disbelief and for mocking God's signs and messengers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the verses as referring to the Quraysh and idol-worshippers, and Ibn Kathir considers the wording general, applying to anyone who worships God in a way that is not accepted while believing he is right. On the identity of 'those who lose most in their deeds', opinions differ: al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that Ali and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas named monks or the People of the Book, while others named the Kharijites. Ibn 'Atiyya rejects these identifications because the verse describes those who deny the meeting with God, which is the trait of idolaters. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that 'weight' may mean value or standing, so they have no esteem with God, whereas al-Razi and al-Nasafi add that no scale is set up for them, since scales are for believing monotheists with good and bad deeds. The commentators agree that mockery adds to the gravity of their denial, since they did more than reject the signs and messengers, they ridiculed them. The hadith narrated by Abu Hurayra, that a corpulent man will not weigh the wing of a mosquito before God, is cited by most of them, and Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as evidence for a literal weighing of deeds.

This verse announces the reward of those who believe and do righteous deeds: the Gardens of Firdaws will be their hospitality, a prepared welcome. The commentators agree that Firdaws refers to the highest, finest and central part of Paradise, and they rely on the hadith that urges asking God for it, as transmitted by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi. On the origin of the word, however, opinions differ. Mujahid and 'Ikrima say it is a garden in Roman or the Abyssinian word for paradise, al-Farra' holds it to be Arabic, while al-Zajjaj thinks it was Arabized from Roman or Syriac. Ka'b and others take it to mean a vineyard, and al-Mubarrad a place of densely grown trees, mostly vines. As for the phrase "they will not desire any removal from it", most read it as meaning they will seek no change, since they find nothing better, while some take it as an emphasis on eternity. Several scholars, including al-Shinqiti and Ibn 'Uthaymin, note that deeds count only when sincere and in line with revelation, and that they lead to Paradise through God's grace.

The verse says that those who believed and did righteous deeds will have the Gardens of Firdaws as their lodging and welcome, dwelling in them forever and not seeking any change from them. The commentators differ on the meaning of Firdaws. Qatada, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan take it to be the highest, central and best part of Paradise, based on the hadith urging believers to ask God for Firdaws. Abu Umama called it the navel of Paradise, Mujahid said it is a garden in the Roman tongue, and Ka'b and al-Dahhak took it to be a garden of grapevines. Al-Zajjaj understood it as the garden that gathers everything found in gardens, while al-Farra' held it to be Arabic. As for the phrase about not desiring a change, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Muqatil explain it as not wishing to move elsewhere. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud read it as not seeking any alternative, since nothing could be better than this abode. Al-Baydawi, al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur also allow that it may mean the negation of any change, which strengthens the sense of eternity. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi note that this expresses the inhabitants' contentment and love, and that eternity does not breed boredom. The commentators then connect the verse to the following verses on the sea and God's words and on sincerity in action, recalling that showing off contradicts such sincerity, as in the report about Jundub ibn Zuhayr cited by al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi.

God declares in this verse that His words, meaning His knowledge, wisdom and what He has made known, never run out. Even if the sea were ink for writing them, it would be exhausted before they were, and the same would hold if a second sea like it were brought. The commentators agree that the 'words' are God's knowledge, His wisdom and the signs that reveal it, and that the finite sea is set against an infinite knowledge so that the image can be grasped. Al-Tabari and Mujahid take the sea as the ink for the pen, while Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand it as the whole sea and the seas that feed it. Ibn Kathir also cites Rabi' ibn Anas, who said that human knowledge compared with God's is like a single drop taken from all the seas. The occasion of revelation, reported by Ibn 'Abbas and given by Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baghawi, al-Wahidi and Ibn 'Atiyya, is that the Jews objected to the verse 'You have been given only a little knowledge', saying they possessed the Torah, which contains everything. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan do not dwell on this. The readers differ on whether the verb 'exhaust' takes the feminine or masculine form and on the vowel of 'madad', variants noted by Abu Hayyan and Ibn al-Jawzi without a firm preference. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir place this verse within the call to monotheism and sincere action that follows it.

God tells His Prophet to say to the polytheists that he is only a human being like them, who does not know the unseen, and that it has been revealed to him that their God is one God with no partner. The verse then states that whoever hopes to meet his Lord, that is, hopes for His reward and fears His punishment, must do righteous work in line with the divine law and must not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord. The commentators agree that the verse sets out the two conditions of accepted works: sincerity toward God and conformity to revelation. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read the word hope sometimes as hope and sometimes as fear, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take it as hoping for a good meeting with God and His approval, and al-Razi understands it as expectation of benefits to come. On association in worship, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid explain it as showing off (riya'), al-Hasan as disbelief, while al-Shawkani and al-Qasimi combine both meanings and stress showing off as the lesser polytheism mentioned in the hadith. Several scholars, including al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, report that the verse was revealed about Jundub ibn Zuhayr, who liked his deeds to be seen, which led the Prophet to say that God does not accept what is shared with another. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi hold that the verse goes beyond showing off and covers every form of association. Mu'awiya is reported to have said it was the last verse revealed, a view Ibn Kathir finds problematic since the surah is Meccan. The core point all agree on is that monotheism and sincerity of intention are the basis of an accepted deed, while the disagreements concern the meaning of hope, of association, and the circumstances of revelation.
